Broad economic gap between the generally wealthier South East of England and many northern regions, visible in incomes, house prices and health.
An economy dominated by services, finance, research and the knowledge sector after the decline of traditional manufacturing and heavy industry.

walkthroughs.body_html:
UK in the 21st Century — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

UK in the 21st Century brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with UK in the 21st Century.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which term describes the UK's rising proportion of people aged 65 and over?
options: Ageing population
Youthful population
Counter-urbanisation
Baby boom

mcqs.q: The UK economy today is dominated by which sector?
options: Services
Heavy manufacturing
Agriculture
Mining

mcqs.q: The 'north-south divide' in the UK refers to differences in what?
options: Average wealth, incomes and house prices between regions
Climate zones only
Languages spoken
Time zones

mcqs.q: Which is an example of UK soft power?
options: The global influence of the BBC and UK universities
The size of the Royal Navy
Threatening trade sanctions
Building military bases abroad

mcqs.q: Does an ageing population only create problems for the UK?
options: The north-south divide is a physical wall separating the regions.
An ageing population means the total population must be falling.
An ageing population is purely an economic burden with no benefits.
No - it raises pension and healthcare costs, but older people also work, volunteer, spend in the economy and provide childcare for families.

mcqs.q: Does the north-south divide mean everywhere in the South is rich and everywhere in the North is poor?
options: The north-south divide is a physical wall separating the regions.
Manufacturing is the largest sector of the UK economy today.
The divide applies uniformly, so all southern places are wealthy and all northern places are deprived.
No - it describes average regional differences in income, investment and house prices; both the North and the South contain wealthy and deprived areas.

mcqs.q: Has manufacturing completely disappeared from the UK economy?
options: Manufacturing is the largest sector of the UK economy today.
Deindustrialisation means the UK no longer makes anything.
An ageing population means the total population must be falling.
No - manufacturing declined relative to services, but the UK still produces high-value goods in industries such as aerospace, pharmaceuticals and cars.
